concepts_used: Legal Basis of EIA: EIA Notification 2006 vs. EIA Notification 1994

solution.concept_anchor: EIA as subordinate legislation under EP Act 1986
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is deceptive because the Environment Protection Act 1986 is the parent legislation and students conflate the parent Act with the notification issued under it, assuming EIA itself must be an Act.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a) — the Environment Protection Act 1986 is the parent legislation; EIA notification is issued under it, not equivalent to it.
Eliminate (c) — there is no standalone 'EIA Act' in India; EIA operates purely through a notification mechanism under Section 3 of EP Act 1986.
Eliminate (d) — Wildlife Protection Act 1972 governs wildlife; it is not the parent legislation for EIA.
Confirm (b) — EIA Notification 2006 is a subordinate legislation (notification) issued under Section 3 of the Environment Protection Act 1986.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Many candidates assume that since EIA is a major regulatory instrument, it must have its own standalone Act. This question exploits that conflation. The EP Act 1986 grants rule-making and notification-issuing power to the Central Government under Section 3; EIA notifications of 1994 and 2006 derive their legal force entirely from this provision. A student who has memorised 'EIA Act' without checking the legal source will choose option (a) confidently but incorrectly.
solution.final_explanation:
The Environmental Impact Assessment framework in India derives its legal authority from the Environment Protection Act (EPA) 1986, specifically through the rule-making power vested in the Central Government under Section 3. The EIA Notification — first issued in 1994 and replaced by the current EIA Notification 2006 — is a subordinate legislation (a statutory notification), not an independent Act of Parliament.

• Option (a): Incorrect. The EP Act 1986 is the parent legislation, not the EIA itself. EIA is issued under it.
• Option (b): Correct. EIA Notification 2006 is a subordinate legislation under Section 3 of the EP Act 1986.
• Option (c): Incorrect. There is no standalone 'Environmental Impact Assessment Act' in India's legislative history.
• Option (d): Incorrect. The Wildlife Protection Act 1972 governs protected areas and wildlife; it has no connection to EIA's legal basis.

Value Addition:
• Section 3 of EP Act 1986 empowers the Centre to take measures to protect and improve environment quality.
• EIA Notification 2006 superseded EIA Notification 1994, introducing Category A/B project classification.
• Being a notification rather than an Act, EIA rules can be amended by the executive without Parliamentary approval — a governance concern raised during Draft EIA 2020 debate.

solution.concept_anchor: Category B2 exemption from EIA but not from Environmental Permission

statement_analysis.statement: Category A projects are appraised by the Expert Appraisal Committee (EAC) under MoEFCC, while Category B projects are appraised by the State-level SEAC under SEIAA.
statement_analysis.reason: Under EIA Notification 2006, Category A projects fall under MoEFCC's EAC, while Category B projects (B1 and B2) fall under SEIAA and SEAC at the state level.

statement_analysis.statement: Category B2 projects are entirely exempt from any form of environmental scrutiny and may commence operations without obtaining any regulatory permission.
statement_analysis.reason: Category B2 projects are exempt from the EIA process but still require Environmental Permission — they are not exempt from all regulatory oversight.

statement_analysis.statement: The classification of a project as Category A or B depends on its scale, location relative to ecologically sensitive areas, and potential impact thresholds.
statement_analysis.reason: EIA Notification 2006 Schedule lists sector-specific thresholds involving capacity, area, and location factors including proximity to ESAs, determining category classification.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) stating all three are correct is deceptive because Statements 1 and 3 are indeed correct, tempting students who have not carefully read Statement 2's absolute claim about 'any form of environmental scrutiny.'
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1 — Category A → EAC/MoEFCC and Category B → SEAC/SEIAA is the correct appraisal authority split under EIA 2006; Statement 1 is correct.
Verify Statement 2 — B2 projects need Environmental Permission even if exempt from full EIA; the claim of exemption from 'any regulatory permission' is false; Statement 2 is incorrect.
Verify Statement 3 — scale, location (ESAs), and impact thresholds are the three criteria for categorisation; Statement 3 is correct.
Only Statements 1 and 3 are correct, pointing to option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap in Statement 2 exploits partial knowledge: candidates know B2 projects are exempt from EIA and assume this means total exemption from regulation. The EIA 2006 framework explicitly requires B2 projects to obtain Environmental Permission even without a full EIA process. The word 'entirely' and 'any form' are scope-extension qualifiers that convert a partially true claim into a false one — a classic UPSC trap design.
solution.final_explanation:
EIA Notification 2006 created a tiered project classification system that determines both the depth of environmental scrutiny and the level of authority responsible for appraisal.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Category A projects, due to their large scale or strategic significance, are appraised by the Expert Appraisal Committee (EAC) under MoEFCC at the national level. Category B projects are handled by State-level SEAC under SEIAA — a key decentralisation feature introduced in 2006.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Category B2 projects are exempted from the full EIA process, but they still require Environmental Permission from the competent authority. They are not free from all environmental regulatory requirements.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The Schedule to EIA 2006 categorises projects based on three criteria: scale of operations, proximity to ecologically sensitive areas (ESAs/CRZ), and sector-specific impact thresholds.

Value Addition:
• Category B1 projects require full EIA and public hearing; B2 projects skip EIA but need Environmental Permission.
• EIA Draft 2020 proposed expanding the B2 exemption category — a major civil society objection.
• A project below Category A thresholds can still become Category A if located within an Ecologically Sensitive Zone.

solution.concept_anchor: Screening not a public stage; Scoping public involvement absent under EIA 2006

statement_analysis.statement: Screening is the stage at which public objections to a proposed project are formally recorded before deciding whether an EIA study is needed.
statement_analysis.reason: Screening is an administrative determination of whether a project needs EIA and its category — it is NOT a public participation stage under EIA 2006.

statement_analysis.statement: Under EIA Notification 2006, public consultation is formally mandated during the Scoping stage to allow communities to influence the Terms of Reference.
statement_analysis.reason: Public consultation is mandated during the Public Hearing stage, NOT during Scoping. The public is not formally involved in determining ToR under the 2006 framework.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) stating only Statement 2 is incorrect would attract candidates who correctly identify Statement 2 as false but wrongly assume Statement 1 describes a valid public-engagement step.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1 — Screening determines whether a project needs EIA and its category; public objections are not formally recorded at this stage; Statement 1 is incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 2 — Formal public involvement under EIA 2006 occurs at Public Hearing, not at Scoping; the statement misattributes public consultation to Scoping; Statement 2 is incorrect.
Both statements are incorrect, pointing to option (d) — 'Both 1 and 2' are NOT correct.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Candidates frequently conflate Screening, Scoping, and Public Hearing because all three involve decisions about the EIA study. Statement 1 sounds plausible because public objections do exist in EIA processes — but they belong to the Public Hearing stage, not Screening. Statement 2 exploits the genuine gap in India's EIA framework: many stakeholders argue the public should be involved in Scoping, and some international systems allow it — but under India's EIA 2006, Scoping is entirely an expert-regulatory process.
solution.final_explanation:
The EIA process under the 2006 notification involves distinct stages with carefully delineated roles for different stakeholders.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: Screening is a purely administrative and technical exercise to determine whether a project requires EIA and to assign it a category (A, B1, or B2). It does not involve any public participation. Projects below prescribed thresholds are automatically classified as B2 at this stage.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Scoping results in the Terms of Reference (ToR) issued by EAC or SEAC within 60 days of the application. This stage is conducted among regulators and technical experts — the public has no formal role during Scoping under EIA Notification 2006. Public consultation occurs later, through the Public Hearing conducted by the State Pollution Control Board.

Value Addition:
• If EAC/SEAC does not issue ToR within 60 days, the proponent may proceed with standardised ToR.
• Baseline data must cover at least one season (excluding monsoon) during Scoping/EIA study preparation.
• Allowing public input at Scoping is an internationally recommended best practice absent from India's current framework — a frequently examined governance gap.

concepts_used: Public Consultation Stage: Public Hearing Mechanism
Exemptions from Public Consultation: Categories and Controversies

solution.concept_anchor: Public hearing: SPCB nodal role; exempted project categories

statement_analysis.statement: Public hearings under EIA 2006 are conducted by the State Pollution Control Board (SPCB) or Union Territory Pollution Control Committee (UTPCC), not by MoEFCC directly.
statement_analysis.reason: EIA 2006 explicitly designates SPCB/UTPCC as the nodal agency for conducting public hearings; MoEFCC is the appraisal authority, not the hearing conductor.

statement_analysis.statement: A minimum 30-day prior public notice is required before conducting a public hearing under EIA 2006, with notification in at least two national and two local newspapers.
statement_analysis.reason: EIA Notification 2006 mandates a 30-day notice period with publication in two national dailies and two local language newspapers, plus notification to the District Collector.

statement_analysis.statement: Projects involving modernisation of irrigation systems and strategic/defence projects are exempted from the public hearing requirement under EIA 2006.
statement_analysis.reason: EIA 2006 Schedule II lists exemptions including strategic/defence projects and modernisation of irrigation projects below prescribed thresholds from public hearing requirements.

statement_analysis.statement: Pipeline and transmission line projects always require a full public hearing regardless of their length or capacity under EIA 2006.
statement_analysis.reason: Pipeline and transmission line projects are among the categories listed as exempted from public hearing under EIA Notification 2006.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) 'Only three' tempts candidates who are uncertain about pipeline exemptions and assume all linear infrastructure requires public hearing due to its widespread environmental footprint.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1 — SPCB/UTPCC as nodal agency for public hearing is explicitly stated in EIA 2006; correct.
Evaluate Statement 2 — 30-day notice in two national + two local newspapers is the prescribed requirement; correct.
Evaluate Statement 3 — Defence/strategic and irrigation modernisation projects are exempted from public hearing in EIA 2006; correct.
Evaluate Statement 4 — Pipeline projects are in fact exempted from public hearing under EIA 2006; the statement claiming they 'always require' a hearing is false.
Three statements are correct (1, 2, 3), pointing to option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 4 is the planted trap. Candidates who know that pipeline projects have significant environmental footprints and are covered under EIA may assume they require public hearing. However, EIA 2006 specifically exempts pipeline and transmission line projects from public hearing — a counter-intuitive provision that has itself attracted controversy. The word 'always' is also a scope-extension signal that alert candidates should flag.
solution.final_explanation:
The Public Consultation stage is the only formal opportunity for affected communities to participate in the EIA process. Its procedural details are heavily tested in UPSC.

• Statement 1 — Correct: SPCB/UTPCC is the designated nodal body for conducting public hearings. MoEFCC's role comes at the appraisal stage after the hearing.
• Statement 2 — Correct: A 30-day mandatory notice period with publication in two national and two local newspapers, and District Collector intimation, ensures adequate advance notification.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Strategic/defence projects and irrigation modernisation below thresholds are statutorily exempted from public hearing to protect national security and avoid delays in water infrastructure.
• Statement 4 — Incorrect: Pipeline and transmission line projects are specifically listed as exempt from public hearing under EIA 2006 — making Statement 4 false.

Value Addition:
• Public hearing must be completed within 45 days of SPCB receiving the request.
• Projects in CRZ areas are also exempted from standalone public hearing under EIA (CRZ has its own process).
• EIA Draft 2020 proposed reducing public response time from 30 to 20 days — a widely criticised rollback.

solution.concept_anchor: EAC advisory role; EC granted by MoEFCC/SEIAA not EAC; EC validity periods
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) incorrectly matches EAC as the EC-granting body (A-1), which is the most common error since students associate EAC with the clearance outcome without distinguishing its advisory role.
elimination_logic: Evaluate A: EAC is described as an advisory committee — it recommends; MoEFCC or SEIAA formally grants EC. A matches with 3 (recommends clearance, does not grant it).
Evaluate B: Environmental Clearance validity is 5 years for construction projects but 10 years for River Valley projects — B matches with 2.
Evaluate C: Half-Yearly Compliance Reports (HYCR) are submitted to MoEFCC and Regional Offices with public disclosure requirement — C matches with 4.
Evaluate D: EC is site-specific and project-specific; transfer to another party requires a fresh application — D matches with 1.
Correct combination is A-3, B-2, C-4, D-1, which is option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The most dangerous trap here is matching A (EAC) with '1 — grants Environmental Clearance.' Students know EAC evaluates projects and associates the name with the EC outcome, overlooking that EAC is strictly advisory. The final EC is issued by MoEFCC (Category A) or SEIAA (Category B). Option (a) exploits this by placing A-1 as the first match — candidates who accept it without verifying get the entire combination wrong.
solution.final_explanation:
The Appraisal stage involves distinct roles across multiple bodies, and the institutional mapping is a recurring UPSC pattern.

**Correct matches:** A-3, B-2, C-4, D-1

• A (Expert Appraisal Committee) — 3: EAC is an advisory body of sectoral and environmental experts. It evaluates EIA reports and public hearing summaries, then recommends grant/rejection. The formal EC is issued by MoEFCC (Category A) or SEIAA (Category B), not by EAC itself.
• B (Validity of Environmental Clearance) — 2: EC is valid for 5 years for the construction phase of most projects, but extended to 10 years for River Valley projects given their long gestation periods.
• C (Half-Yearly Compliance Reports) — 4: Post-clearance monitoring requires project proponents to submit HYCRs to MoEFCC/Regional Offices, and these must be placed in the public domain.
• D (Site and party specificity of EC) — 1: EC is tied to both the specific project site and the specific applicant. Any change in party requires a fresh application — EC is non-transferable.

Value Addition:
• EAC is chaired by an independent expert, not a government secretary.
• 'Deemed approval' does NOT apply to EC — silence by authority is not approval.
• Corporate Environment Responsibility (CER) is mandated in EC conditions — distinct from CSR under Companies Act.

solution.concept_anchor: Deemed EC inapplicability; post-facto EC prohibition
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is deceptive because both A and R are factually true, tempting students to select (a) without checking whether R causally explains A — it does not, as the prohibition on deemed EC and the prohibition on post-facto EC arise from different legal principles.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? — Yes. Under EIA 2006, failure of the authority to respond within prescribed time does NOT constitute deemed Environmental Clearance, unlike some other regulatory frameworks in India.

Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? — Yes. The Supreme Court in Alembic Pharmaceuticals vs. Rohit Prajapati (2020) explicitly reaffirmed that post-facto EC is impermissible; EIA 2006 does not provide for it.

Step 3: Does R causally explain A? — No. The absence of deemed EC is a separate principle about regulatory silence, not about post-facto clearance for projects that commenced without EC. These are two distinct rules addressing different scenarios: one covers delayed regulatory response; the other covers projects started illegally without clearance.
Both A and R are correct but R does NOT explain A — correct option is (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Both the assertion and reason reference the EIA framework's non-approval defaults, making them appear causally linked. A partially prepared candidate hears 'post-facto EC is not permitted' and immediately connects it to 'therefore silence is not deemed approval' — but these are distinct principles. Deemed approval doctrine concerns administrative silence on a pending application; post-facto clearance concerns projects already commenced illegally. The causal link between them is absent.
solution.final_explanation:
Two important but distinct protective principles operate in India's EC framework.

**Assertion (A):** Correct. Unlike some licensing regimes where regulatory inaction within a prescribed period constitutes deemed approval, Environmental Clearance under EIA 2006 carries no such provision. Silence by MoEFCC or SEIAA cannot be construed as EC — the project proponent must obtain an explicit written clearance.

**Reason (R):** Correct. The Supreme Court in Alembic Pharmaceuticals vs. Rohit Prajapati (2020) firmly held that post-facto Environmental Clearance — granting EC after a project has already commenced construction or operations — is constitutionally impermissible as it violates the precautionary principle and renders the EIA process meaningless.

**Causal relationship:** R does NOT explain A. 'Deemed EC' addresses administrative silence on a pending application from a proponent who has not yet started the project. 'Post-facto EC' addresses a proponent who started without any EC. These are separate legal questions arising from different factual situations, governed by different principles.

Correct answer: (b) — Both A and R are correct, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.

Value Addition:
• EIA Draft 2020's Clause 26 proposed allowing post-facto clearance — rejected by courts and civil society.
• EP Act 1986 penalties: up to 5 years imprisonment and/or ₹1 lakh fine, extendable by ₹5,000/day.
• NGT can impose penalties and order closure independently of criminal proceedings under EP Act.

solution.concept_anchor: Chronological evolution of EIA framework and key developments
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) places the EIA Draft 2020 before NGT's establishment (2010), which seems plausible to a student who knows EIA 2006 came first but confuses the 2020 Draft with any interim amendments.
elimination_logic: Anchor the earliest event: EIA Notification 1994 was the first mandatory EIA framework — this must come first.
EIA Notification 2006 replaced the 1994 notification — it comes second.
NGT Act 2010 established the National Green Tribunal — it comes after EIA 2006.
Parivesh Portal was launched in 2018 as a single-window clearance system — it comes after NGT 2010.
EIA Draft 2020 is the most recent development in the sequence.
Correct sequence: 1994 → 2006 → 2010 → 2018 → 2020, matching option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap in options (b) and (c) involves swapping the NGT Act 2010 and Parivesh Portal 2018. Students who know both institutions but have not fixed their dates may place Parivesh before NGT or conflate intermediate EIA amendments with standalone events. Option (d) places the 1994 notification after 2006, which is obviously wrong but included as the elimination anchor.
solution.final_explanation:
Understanding the chronological evolution of India's EIA framework helps map the expanding regulatory architecture.

**Correct sequence:** EIA Notification 1994 → EIA Notification 2006 → NGT Act 2010 → Parivesh Portal Launch 2018 → EIA Draft Notification 2020

• **1994:** First mandatory EIA notification in India — made EIA compulsory for 29 categories of projects; applied only at central level.
• **2006:** Comprehensive replacement — introduced Category A/B distinction, decentralised to state level (SEIAA/SEAC), formalised public hearing through SPCB.
• **2010:** NGT Act established the National Green Tribunal with appellate jurisdiction over EC orders under Section 16.
• **2018:** Parivesh Portal launched as a single-window digital platform integrating EC, FC, CRZ, and Wildlife clearance applications.
• **2020:** Draft EIA Notification 2020 proposed controversial changes including post-facto EC (Clause 26) and reduced public consultation period — remained a draft as of the knowledge cutoff.

• Option (b): Incorrect — places NGT after EIA Draft 2020.
• Option (c): Incorrect — inverts Parivesh and NGT.
• Option (d): Incorrect — places 1994 notification after 2006.

Value Addition:
• Parivesh does not eliminate separate clearances — it is a common application portal only.
• EIA 1994 was the pre-decentralisation era; appraisal was centralised at MoEFCC.
• NGT's Section 16 allows appeal within 30 days of EC grant.

concepts_used: Coastal Regulation Zone (CRZ) Notification and EIA Interface
Ecologically Sensitive Areas (ESA)/Ecologically Sensitive Zones (ESZ) and EIA Categorization

solution.concept_anchor: ESZ location escalates project to Category A; dual clearance for CRZ + Category A
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) stating the project qualifies as Category B1 tempts candidates who correctly identify it as a mid-scale thermal plant but overlook the ESZ location trigger that escalates it to Category A.
elimination_logic: Identify the critical fact: the project is located within the Ecologically Sensitive Zone of a National Park — this location trigger automatically escalates any project to Category A regardless of its scale.
Eliminate (a) — Category B1 applies to projects meeting scale thresholds without ESZ location; ESZ location overrides scale-based B1 classification.
Eliminate (b) — CRZ clearance applies to coastal regulation zones; the scenario describes an ESZ, not a CRZ location.
Eliminate (d) — The project is not exempt from EIA merely because it is mid-scale; ESZ projects face more stringent scrutiny, not less.
Confirm (c) — ESZ location makes the project Category A (MoEFCC/EAC appraisal), and the project also needs Forest Clearance under Forest Conservation Act 1980 if forest land is involved.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scenario is designed to separate knowledge of scale-based thresholds (which would suggest Category B1) from knowledge of location-based escalation rules (ESZ → Category A). A student who has memorised sector-specific thresholds without understanding the ESZ override rule will confidently select (a). This is a precision-knowledge trap testing the 'regardless of size' clause for ESZ-located projects.
solution.final_explanation:
EIA Notification 2006 provides that certain location characteristics automatically escalate a project's category irrespective of its scale. Projects located within Ecologically Sensitive Zones (ESZs) — declared buffer areas around Protected Areas — are classified as Category A and appraised by EAC under MoEFCC, even if their capacity would ordinarily place them in Category B.

In this scenario:
- A 200 MW thermal plant would normally be assessed on sectoral thresholds, potentially qualifying as Category B1.
- However, its location within the ESZ of a National Park triggers the location-based escalation rule → Category A → MoEFCC/EAC appraisal.
- Additionally, if the project involves forest land, a separate Forest Clearance under the Forest Conservation Act 1980 is required concurrently.

• Option (a): Incorrect — ESZ location overrides scale-based B1 classification.
• Option (b): Incorrect — CRZ clearance is for coastal projects; this is an ESZ scenario.
• Option (c): Correct — ESZ location → Category A, plus Forest Clearance if forest land is involved.
• Option (d): Incorrect — ESZ-located projects face heightened scrutiny, not exemption.

Value Addition:
• Supreme Court in T.N. Godavarman case mandated a minimum 10 km ESZ around all National Parks/Wildlife Sanctuaries as an interim measure.
• Stage I Forest Clearance (in-principle) can be obtained concurrently with EC; Stage II only after EC grant.
• Two-window clearance (EC + FC) is now processed through the Parivesh single-window portal.

concepts_used: Strategic Environmental Assessment (SEA): Concept and India's Gap
Cumulative Impact Assessment (CIA): Concept vs. Indian Practice

solution.concept_anchor: SEA applies to policies/plans/programmes; CIA is project-cluster tool
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) 'Cumulative Impact Assessment' is the strongest distractor because it, like SEA, goes beyond single-project evaluation and students conflate the two as both being 'upstream' tools.
elimination_logic: Identify the common attribute: three of the four are tools that assess environmental impacts BEYOND a single project in isolation.
SEA — applies to policies, plans, and programmes (PPPs) — broader than project-level, clearly in the group.
CIA — assesses combined impacts of multiple projects in a basin/region — beyond single-project, fits the group.
Integrated Coastal Zone Management (ICZM) — a planning approach for entire coastal zones, beyond single-project, fits the group.
Environmental Management Plan (EMP) — this is a project-specific mitigation and monitoring document prepared as part of a single project's EIA report — it is the odd one out.
Correct answer: (b) EMP.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: EMP sounds like a planning-level tool due to its name, and candidates who have not studied its precise role in the EIA process may group it with SEA, CIA, and ICZM as a broader environmental governance instrument. In reality, EMP is prepared by the project proponent as part of the individual project's EIA report — it is entirely project-specific and forms a schedule of the EC conditions.
solution.final_explanation:
This question tests understanding of which tools operate at the policy/regional/multi-project scale versus the single-project scale.

• Option (a) Strategic Environmental Assessment (SEA): Operates upstream of project-level EIA — applies to policies, plans, and programmes (PPPs). Mandated in the EU; absent in India's legal framework. Goes beyond any single project.
• Option (b) Environment Management Plan (EMP): Prepared by the project proponent as part of the EIA report for a specific project. It specifies mitigation measures, monitoring framework, and institutional arrangements. It is entirely project-specific — the ODD ONE OUT.
• Option (c) Cumulative Impact Assessment (CIA): Evaluates the combined environmental impacts of multiple projects in a region or river basin. Broader than individual project EIA — Supreme Court ordered CIA for Ganga tributaries after Uttarakhand 2013.
• Option (d) Integrated Coastal Zone Management (ICZM): A SEA-like planning approach for managing entire coastal zones holistically — World Bank-supported in India.

Value Addition:
• EMP is a legally binding schedule attached to the EC — non-compliance is actionable.
• CIA is not mandatory under EIA 2006 — a significant governance gap.
• CER (Corporate Environment Responsibility) specified in EMP is 2% of project cost — distinct from CSR under Companies Act.

concepts_used: Accreditation of EIA Consultants: QCI-NABET System

solution.concept_anchor: QCI non-statutory character; NABET accreditation mandatory since 2010

statement_analysis.statement: Since 2010, only EIA consultancy organisations accredited by NABET under the Quality Council of India (QCI) are permitted to prepare EIA reports for Category A and B1 projects.
statement_analysis.reason: MoEFCC made NABET-QCI accreditation mandatory for EIA consultants from 2010 onwards, applying to Category A and B1 projects requiring full EIA.

statement_analysis.statement: The Quality Council of India (QCI) is a statutory body established by an Act of Parliament, giving its accreditations the force of law.
statement_analysis.reason: QCI is a non-statutory, non-profit body set up jointly by the Government of India and industry associations (CII, FICCI, ASSOCHAM) — it does not derive authority from a Parliamentary statute.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) claiming both statements are correct is deceptive because Statement 1 is clearly correct and many students assume QCI must be statutory since its accreditations are mandatory in a government-regulated process.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1 — NABET-QCI accreditation has been mandatory for Category A and B1 EIA consultants since 2010; Statement 1 is correct.
Evaluate Statement 2 — QCI is not a statutory body; it was set up as a non-profit by Government of India and industry associations (CII, FICCI, ASSOCHAM); Statement 2 is incorrect.
Statement 1 correct, Statement 2 incorrect — option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap exploits the assumption that if a body's accreditations are mandated in a government notification, the body itself must have statutory character. QCI is one of India's few non-statutory bodies whose certifications are referenced in mandatory regulatory frameworks. NABET is a division of QCI, and its accreditation is cited in MoEFCC's EIA framework — but QCI itself was constituted through an executive resolution, not legislation.
solution.final_explanation:
The accreditation system for EIA consultants introduced a quality-control mechanism within the EIA process, but its institutional foundation has an important non-statutory character.

• Statement 1 — Correct: From 2010, the MoEFCC made it mandatory that EIA reports for Category A and B1 projects be prepared only by NABET-accredited consultancy organisations. This addressed concerns about EIA report quality and institutional capacity.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: QCI is not a statutory body. It was established in 1997 as a non-profit organisation through a joint initiative of the Government of India and three apex industry associations — CII, FICCI, and ASSOCHAM. It has no parent Act of Parliament. Its accreditations carry regulatory weight through references in government notifications, not through inherent statutory authority.

Value Addition:
• A structural bias exists in EIA: the project proponent hires and pays the EIA consultant — creating potential conflict of interest.
• NABET accredits organisations, not individuals — the firm as a whole must meet quality standards.
• QCI also runs the India Quality Award and accredits institutions in education, healthcare, and testing sectors beyond EIA.

solution.concept_anchor: ToR issued within 60 days; baseline data minimum one season excluding monsoon
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) '30 days / any two seasons' is deceptive because 30 days appears in the EIA framework (public notice period for Public Hearing) and students may transpose it to the ToR timeline.
elimination_logic: Recall that the ToR issuance timeline under EIA 2006 is 60 days — not 30 days (public notice) or 90 days (a fabricated extension period).
Recall that baseline data must cover a minimum of one season, explicitly excluding monsoon season due to data quality concerns.
Option (c) correctly pairs both: 60 days for ToR issuance and one season (excluding monsoon) for baseline data.
Eliminate (a) — 30 days is the public hearing notice period, not ToR timeline; eliminate (b) — 90 days is fabricated; eliminate (d) — 45 days is the SPCB public hearing completion timeline.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The 30-day figure appears multiple times in EIA 2006 (public notice period, NGT appeal period) and candidates who have not carefully separated different timelines will substitute it for the 60-day ToR issuance period. The monsoon exclusion for baseline data is a precise procedural detail that distinguishes thorough preparation from surface-level recall.
solution.final_explanation:
The Scoping stage establishes the Terms of Reference (ToR) that govern the depth and scope of the EIA study.

• Option (a): Incorrect — 30 days applies to public notice for public hearing, not ToR issuance; 'any two seasons' misrepresents the baseline data requirement.
• Option (b): Incorrect — 90 days for ToR is fabricated; no such provision exists in EIA 2006.
• Option (c): Correct — EAC/SEAC must issue ToR within 60 days of receiving the Form 1/PFR from the proponent. Baseline environmental data must cover a minimum of one full season, with monsoon season excluded (due to data distortion from flooding and seasonal variation).
• Option (d): Incorrect — 45 days is the timeline for SPCB to complete public hearing after receiving the request, not for ToR issuance.

Value Addition:
• If EAC/SEAC fails to issue ToR within 60 days, the proponent may proceed using standardised ToR.
• Baseline data collection is typically done by the EIA consultant during the Scoping/EIA study phase.
• The monsoon exclusion is designed to ensure representative ambient air, water, and ecological data collection.

solution.concept_anchor: NGT Section 16 appeal period 30 days; locus standi any aggrieved person
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) pairing NGT with 60-day appeal period is deceptive because 60 days appears in the EIA scoping stage (ToR issuance) and candidates may transpose it to the NGT appeal window.
elimination_logic: Recall that NGT Act 2010, Section 16 provides for appeal against EC orders within 30 days of the EC being granted.
Option (a) correctly pairs 'NGT Act 2010, Section 16' with '30-day appeal window for aggrieved persons against EC orders' — this is correct.
Option (b) is incorrect — 60 days is the ToR issuance timeline, not the NGT appeal period.
Option (c) is incorrect — locus standi at NGT is broader ('any aggrieved person'), not restricted to directly displaced communities only.
Option (d) is incorrect — NGT does not have exclusive jurisdiction over all environmental matters; High Courts retain writ jurisdiction and there are concurrent jurisdiction debates.
solution.final_explanation:
The NGT's role as an appellate authority over Environmental Clearance decisions is a critical governance feature frequently tested.

• Option (a): Correct. Section 16 of the NGT Act 2010 allows any person aggrieved by an order or award including grant of EC to appeal to the NGT within 30 days. The locus standi is broad — 'any aggrieved person,' not just directly displaced or affected parties.
• Option (b): Incorrect. The 60-day figure applies to ToR issuance by EAC/SEAC during the Scoping stage — not to the NGT appeal period.
• Option (c): Incorrect. NGT's locus standi is broader than courts — it extends to any aggrieved person, not just those facing direct physical displacement or land acquisition.
• Option (d): Incorrect. High Courts retain writ jurisdiction on constitutional questions; there is an ongoing legal debate about concurrent jurisdiction between NGT and High Courts on EIA matters.

Value Addition:
• NGT Act 2010 was established under the principle of sustainable development, precautionary principle, and polluter pays principle.
• NGT can impose penalties and direct project closure independently of criminal proceedings under EP Act 1986.
• Landmark NGT orders include the Vedanta Alumina case (public hearing validity) and Mopa Airport case.

Environment Management Plan (EMP): Mitigation and Monitoring Framework

solution.concept_anchor: EIA Report as input not decision; EMP prepared by proponent; CER vs CSR distinction

statement_analysis.statement: The EIA Report constitutes the final regulatory decision on a project; once submitted to MoEFCC, it confers Environmental Clearance on the project proponent.
statement_analysis.reason: The EIA Report is an input document for the appraisal process. Environmental Clearance is granted by MoEFCC or SEIAA after appraisal by EAC/SEAC — the Report itself does not grant clearance.

statement_analysis.statement: The Environment Management Plan (EMP) is prepared by the project proponent, not the regulatory authority, and upon grant of EC it becomes a legally binding schedule of conditions.
statement_analysis.reason: Under EIA 2006, the proponent prepares the EMP as part of the EIA report. The EMP's conditions are incorporated into the EC as binding compliance requirements.

statement_analysis.statement: Corporate Environment Responsibility (CER) mandated in Environmental Clearance conditions requires allocation of 2% of project cost for local area development, and is a distinct obligation from CSR under the Companies Act 2013.
statement_analysis.reason: CER is an MoEFCC-mandated condition in EC, tied to the specific project's environmental footprint and local community; CSR under Companies Act applies to the company's overall net profit — they are separate legal obligations.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) selecting only Statement 3 tempts candidates who correctly reject Statement 1 but are uncertain about whether EMP is actually prepared by the proponent or the regulator.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1 — EIA Report is an input to appraisal; EC is granted separately by MoEFCC/SEIAA; Statement 1 is incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 2 — EMP is prepared by the proponent as part of EIA; it becomes binding upon EC grant; Statement 2 is correct.
Evaluate Statement 3 — CER (2% of project cost, EC-linked) is distinct from CSR (Companies Act, profit-linked); Statement 3 is correct.
Statements 2 and 3 are correct — option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 exploits the common confusion between EIA Report submission and EC grant. Many candidates treat the report submission as effectively equivalent to clearance, not realising that the appraisal stage (EAC review, public hearing outcomes, EAC recommendation, and final MoEFCC/SEIAA decision) follows report submission. Statement 2's trap is the regulator-vs-proponent confusion — students assume regulators write EMP, whereas the proponent proposes mitigation measures and the regulator evaluates them.
solution.final_explanation:
The EIA Report and the EC are distinct instruments with different legal characters, and the EMP occupies a specific place in this architecture.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: The EIA Report is an input document submitted by the proponent after completing the baseline study and public hearing. It initiates the Appraisal stage. Environmental Clearance is issued by MoEFCC (Category A) or SEIAA (Category B) only after the EAC/SEAC evaluates the report and makes a recommendation.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The EMP is developed by the project proponent and forms part of the EIA report. It details mitigation measures, monitoring protocols, institutional responsibilities, and financial provisions. Upon EC grant, the EMP's key commitments are incorporated as binding EC conditions.
• Statement 3 — Correct: CER is mandated through EC conditions by MoEFCC — approximately 2% of project cost directed toward local area environmental and community development. This is legally and procedurally separate from CSR obligations under Section 135 of the Companies Act 2013, which is triggered by company profitability thresholds.

Value Addition:
• EIA Report must include an executive summary in the local language for public hearing accessibility.
• Only NABET-QCI accredited consultants can prepare the EIA report for Category A and B1 projects.
• Risk assessment is a mandatory component of the EIA report for hazardous industry categories.

solution.concept_anchor: Parivesh Portal — common application portal, not merger of clearances
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) claiming Parivesh merges all clearances into a single unified clearance is deceptive because the portal's name and design suggest integration, leading candidates to assume legal merger rather than administrative integration.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a) — Parivesh is a common application portal; each clearance (EC, FC, CRZ, Wildlife) remains legally independent.
Eliminate (c) — Stage II Forest Clearance can only be obtained AFTER EC is granted, not concurrently with Stage I and EC.
Eliminate (d) — Parivesh was launched in 2018, not 2015; the year attribution is a temporal-swap trap.
Confirm (b) — Parivesh provides a single-window digital interface for applying for multiple clearances concurrently, but each clearance is processed independently by the respective authority.
solution.final_explanation:
The Parivesh Portal represents an administrative reform in India's clearance ecosystem without altering the legal independence of individual clearances.

• Option (a): Incorrect. Parivesh does not merge Environmental Clearance, Forest Clearance, CRZ Clearance, and Wildlife Clearance into one unified document. Each retains its distinct legal character under separate statutes (EP Act, Forest Conservation Act, CRZ Notification, Wildlife Protection Act).
• Option (b): Correct. Launched in 2018, Parivesh (Pro-Active and Responsive facilitation by Interactive, Virtuous and Environmental Single-window Hub) provides a common digital application platform integrating EC, FC, CRZ, and Wildlife clearance applications — enabling concurrent processing and reducing delays.
• Option (c): Incorrect. Stage I Forest Clearance (in-principle approval) can be obtained concurrently with the EC process. However, Stage II Forest Clearance (final approval for diversion of forest land) can only be granted after EC is obtained — the sequence is Stage I concurrent with EC → EC granted → Stage II FC.
• Option (d): Incorrect. Parivesh was launched in 2018, not 2015.

Value Addition:
• Before Parivesh, sequential clearance requirement caused significant project delays — forest clearance had to precede EC in some interpretations.
• Parivesh was developed by NIC (National Informatics Centre) under MoEFCC.
• Each authority (MoEFCC for EC, Forest department for FC) retains its independent decision-making under Parivesh.

solution.concept_anchor: CIA not mandatory under EIA 2006; SEA not legally mandated in India

statement_analysis.statement: Cumulative Impact Assessment (CIA) is a mandatory stage in India's EIA Notification 2006, requiring assessment of combined impacts of all projects in a river basin before any individual project clearance is granted.
statement_analysis.reason: CIA is NOT a mandatory stage under EIA 2006. Projects are assessed individually. The Supreme Court ordered CIA for Ganga tributaries as an ad hoc measure following the Uttarakhand disaster of 2013, but this does not make CIA a standard EIA 2006 requirement.

statement_analysis.statement: Strategic Environmental Assessment (SEA) is legally mandated in India for all policy decisions affecting natural resources, bringing India's framework in line with the EU's SEA Directive 2001.
statement_analysis.reason: SEA is NOT legally mandated in India. India lacks an SEA law or policy, making it a recognised governance gap. The EU SEA Directive 2001 mandates SEA for plans and programmes — India has not adopted an equivalent instrument.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) claiming only Statement 2 is incorrect tempts candidates who know SEA is absent in India but incorrectly believe CIA was made mandatory after the 2013 Uttarakhand disaster following the Supreme Court order.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1 — CIA is not a mandatory stage under EIA 2006; Supreme Court's order was for Ganga tributaries specifically, not a general statutory mandate; Statement 1 is incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 2 — India has no SEA law; the EU SEA Directive 2001 exists but India has not adopted an equivalent; Statement 2 is incorrect.
Both statements are NOT correct — option (c) 'Both 1 and 2' are not correct.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 exploits the Uttarakhand 2013 disaster context. Students who know the Supreme Court directed CIA studies for Ganga tributaries may assume this created a general statutory mandate. It did not — it was a court-directed study for a specific region. Statement 2 exploits awareness of the EU SEA Directive: candidates who know India is moving toward SEA may assume it has already been legally mandated, when in reality SEA remains the standard answer to 'what is missing from India's EIA framework.'
solution.final_explanation:
Two significant governance gaps in India's EIA framework are tested here.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: EIA Notification 2006 does not include CIA as a mandatory stage. Individual projects are assessed in isolation even when multiple projects exist in the same river basin or region. The Supreme Court's direction to MoEFCC to commission CIA studies for Alaknanda and Bhagirathi tributaries after the 2013 Uttarakhand floods was project/region-specific judicial intervention — not a general statutory mandate.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: India does not have a legally enforceable SEA framework. SEA applies EIA principles upstream — to policies, plans, and programmes (PPPs) like coal block allocation, highway development plans, or river interlinking proposals. The EU SEA Directive 2001 established this as a legal requirement in Europe; India has no equivalent legislation, making SEA a frequently cited governance gap in UPSC answers.

Value Addition:
• Examples where SEA would be most relevant in India: National Highway development plans, Coal Block allocation policy, and National River Linking Programme.
• CIA ≠ a cumulative chapter in an individual EIA report — CIA is a basin-level planning tool.
• ICZM (Integrated Coastal Zone Management) is the closest SEA-like instrument India has implemented, supported by the World Bank.

solution.concept_anchor: River valley project: Category A threshold; 10-year EC validity; mandatory studies

statement_analysis.statement: All river valley projects with installed capacity of 50 MW or more, or with a submergence area of 10,000 hectares or more, are classified as Category A regardless of which state they are located in.
statement_analysis.reason: EIA 2006 Schedule lists river valley projects ≥50 MW or ≥10,000 ha submergence as Category A — the inter-state or intra-state location does not affect this classification.

statement_analysis.statement: Environmental Clearance granted for river valley projects remains valid for 10 years for the construction phase, compared to 5 years for most other project categories.
statement_analysis.reason: EIA 2006 specifically provides extended EC validity of 10 years for river valley projects (vs. 5 years for others) given the longer construction and commissioning timelines of large dams and hydropower stations.

statement_analysis.statement: A mandatory Cumulative Impact Assessment is required before any individual river valley project can receive Environmental Clearance under EIA Notification 2006.
statement_analysis.reason: CIA is not a mandatory statutory requirement under EIA 2006. While courts have ordered CIA for specific river basins, it is not a standard prerequisite for individual project EC.

statement_analysis.statement: Environmental Clearance for river valley projects must include assessment of downstream flow impacts, fisheries effects, and Resettlement and Rehabilitation plans for displaced communities.
statement_analysis.reason: EIA 2006 and MoEFCC sector-specific guidelines for river valley projects mandate studies including carrying capacity, downstream flow assessment, fisheries impact, and displacement/R&R plan as mandatory components.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) 'Only two' tempts candidates who correctly reject Statement 3 but are uncertain about whether downstream flow assessment and R&R plans are mandated in the EC process or only in separate R&R legislation.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1 — ≥50 MW or ≥10,000 ha submergence = Category A regardless of state; correct.
Evaluate Statement 2 — 10-year EC validity for river valley vs. 5 years for others; correct.
Evaluate Statement 3 — CIA is not a mandatory EIA 2006 stage; court-ordered for specific basins only; incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 4 — Downstream flow, fisheries, R&R are mandated in river valley sector-specific EIA guidelines; correct.
Three statements correct (1, 2, 4) — option (a) 'Only three' is not listed; re-check options. Options are: (a) Only one, (b) Only two, (c) Only three, (d) All four. Three are correct — option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 exploits knowledge of the Uttarakhand 2013 disaster and subsequent Supreme Court directions, which may make candidates believe CIA is now mandatory for all river valley projects. In reality, it remains a judicially-directed requirement for specific basins, not a general statutory mandate under EIA 2006.
solution.final_explanation:
River valley and hydropower projects receive special treatment under India's EIA framework due to their large-scale and irreversible impacts.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The 50 MW capacity or 10,000 ha submergence threshold for Category A classification applies regardless of state boundaries, ensuring national-level appraisal for large projects.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Given the multi-year construction timelines of dams and hydropower stations, EIA 2006 provides 10-year EC validity for river valley projects — double the standard 5-year validity for other categories.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: CIA is not a mandatory pre-condition for individual river valley project EC under EIA 2006. While the Supreme Court directed CIA studies for specific river systems (Alaknanda-Bhagirathi post-2013), this is not a generalised statutory requirement.
• Statement 4 — Correct: MoEFCC's sector-specific EIA guidelines for river valley projects mandate carrying capacity studies, downstream environmental flow assessments, fisheries impact studies, and comprehensive Resettlement and Rehabilitation plans.

Three statements (1, 2, 4) are correct — option (c).

Value Addition:
• The Uttarakhand flash floods of 2013 reignited the debate on cumulative impacts of multiple hydropower projects on Ganga tributaries.
• NGT issued interim stays on several Uttarakhand hydropower projects pending CIA completion.
• EC for river valley projects is always Category A — appraised by EAC (River Valley) under MoEFCC.

solution.concept_anchor: Post-facto clearance in Draft 2020 Clause 26; Supreme Court prohibition on post-facto EC
solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) claiming A is incorrect would attract candidates who confuse the proposal of post-facto EC in Draft 2020 (which has not been finalised) with the existing legal position — they may think post-facto EC is already permitted.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? — Yes. EIA Draft Notification 2020's Clause 26 proposed a mechanism for regularising projects that commenced without prior Environmental Clearance — termed 'post-facto clearance,' a provision that drew widespread criticism from civil society and environmentalists.

Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? — Yes. The Supreme Court in Alembic Pharmaceuticals vs. Rohit Prajapati (2020) held that post-facto EC is constitutionally impermissible; EIA 2006 does not permit it; the precautionary principle under environmental law demands prior assessment.

Step 3: Does R causally explain A? — Yes. The reason the proposal in Draft 2020 was so controversial is precisely because the Supreme Court had already held post-facto EC to be illegal. R explains why A (the proposal) was met with intense criticism and why the draft remained unfinalized.
Both A and R are correct AND R explains A — correct option is (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (d) is the primary trap: candidates who know EIA 2006 does not allow post-facto EC, and who have not tracked the Draft 2020's proposals carefully, may think Assertion A itself is incorrect — assuming post-facto clearance was never proposed. In fact, Clause 26 of Draft EIA 2020 did explicitly propose post-facto regularisation. The Reason correctly anchors the legal prohibition. This question requires distinguishing between what the law currently is, what was proposed, and what the courts have said.
solution.final_explanation:
The EIA Draft Notification 2020 represented a significant proposed rollback of India's environmental governance, and Clause 26 on post-facto clearance was its most contested element.

**Assertion (A):** Correct. Clause 26 of the EIA Draft 2020 proposed allowing projects that had commenced operations without obtaining prior Environmental Clearance to apply for regularisation — effectively creating a mechanism for 'post-facto' or retroactive EC. This was criticised as incentivising violations by making violation the pathway to regularisation.

**Reason (R):** Correct. The Supreme Court in Alembic Pharmaceuticals vs. Rohit Prajapati (2020) unequivocally held that post-facto Environmental Clearance is impermissible. The Court reasoned that EIA requires prior assessment of impacts — assessing impacts after construction or operations have commenced defeats the entire purpose of the process and violates the precautionary principle.

**Causal link:** R directly explains why A is controversial — the Supreme Court's ruling meant that Clause 26 of Draft 2020 directly contradicted binding judicial precedent, making it constitutionally vulnerable and the central objection to its enactment.

Correct answer: (a)

Value Addition:
• EIA Draft 2020 also proposed reducing the public response period from 30 to 20 days.
• Draft 2020 remained unfinalized as of the knowledge cutoff; EIA Notification 2006 remains operative.
• EP Act 1986 penalties: up to 5 years imprisonment and ₹1 lakh fine for violations — extendable by ₹5,000/day for continuing violations.

solution.concept_anchor: CRZ + EIA dual clearance for Category A coastal projects

statement_analysis.statement: A project located in the Coastal Regulation Zone (CRZ) that also qualifies as a Category A project under EIA Notification 2006 requires both CRZ Clearance and Environmental Clearance from MoEFCC.
statement_analysis.reason: Category A projects within CRZ require dual clearance — CRZ clearance under the CRZ Notification and Environmental Clearance under EIA 2006 — both granted by MoEFCC.

statement_analysis.statement: Under CRZ Notification 2019, the No Development Zone width along open coastlines was increased compared to CRZ Notification 2011 to strengthen coastal protection.
statement_analysis.reason: CRZ Notification 2019 actually reduced NDZ requirements in some categories (e.g., for densely populated rural areas) and relaxed development norms for tourism — it did not uniformly increase NDZ widths.

statement_analysis.statement: The Integrated Coastal Zone Management (ICZM) approach represents an attempt to apply strategic, region-level environmental assessment to coastal areas beyond individual project clearances.
statement_analysis.reason: ICZM is a holistic, SEA-like planning approach for managing entire coastal zones, addressing cumulative impacts, ecosystem services, and long-term coastal sustainability — supported by World Bank projects in India.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) claiming all three statements are correct is the primary distractor, since Statement 2 sounds plausible — students may assume CRZ 2019 strengthened (rather than relaxed) coastal protections, given public awareness of coastal erosion concerns.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1 — Category A projects in CRZ require both CRZ clearance and EC from MoEFCC (dual clearance); correct.
Evaluate Statement 2 — CRZ 2019 relaxed NDZ requirements in some coastal categories, it did not increase NDZ widths uniformly; incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 3 — ICZM is a region-level strategic approach for coastal zones, supported by World Bank in India; correct.
Statements 1 and 3 correct, Statement 2 incorrect — option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 is the planted trap exploiting the assumption that newer environmental notifications must be more protective than older ones. CRZ 2019 was in fact criticised for diluting protections — including NDZ reductions for densely populated villages and increased tourism activity permissions. A candidate who associates 'new notification = stronger protection' will incorrectly mark Statement 2 as correct.
solution.final_explanation:
The interface between CRZ regulations and the EIA framework creates one of the most complex clearance landscapes in Indian environmental governance.

• Statement 1 — Correct: When a project falls within the CRZ and is also Category A under EIA 2006, it requires dual clearance: CRZ Clearance (under CRZ Notification) AND Environmental Clearance (under EIA 2006). Both are granted by MoEFCC at the national level for Category A projects.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: CRZ Notification 2019 introduced several relaxations, including reduced NDZ widths for densely populated rural coastal areas and expanded tourism and infrastructure permissions. It did not uniformly increase coastal protection widths — critics argued it diluted coastal protections.
• Statement 3 — Correct: ICZM is India's closest analog to Strategic Environmental Assessment for coastal areas. World Bank-supported ICZM projects in Gujarat, Odisha, and West Bengal attempt to manage entire coastal ecosystems, addressing cumulative pressures rather than individual project impacts.

Value Addition:
• CRZ 2019 also introduced island development policies for Lakshadweep and Andaman — previously restricted.
• MoEFCC grants CRZ clearance; SCZMA (State Coastal Zone Management Authority) handles lower-category cases.
• CRZ projects in certain categories are exempted from standard EIA public hearing — CRZ has its own public participation mechanism.

solution.concept_anchor: Key shifts from EIA 1994 to EIA 2006: decentralisation and category system
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) placing decentralisation before the Category A/B system implies they were introduced separately in EIA 2006, tempting candidates who studied each feature independently without knowing they were co-introduced.
elimination_logic: Anchor fact 1: EIA Notification 1994 introduced mandatory EIA in India — this is the starting point.
Anchor fact 2: EIA 2006 introduced BOTH the Category A/B system AND decentralisation to SEIAA/SEAC simultaneously — they are co-features of the 2006 notification.
Anchor fact 3: NABET-QCI accreditation for consultants became mandatory in 2010 — after EIA 2006.
Anchor fact 4: Parivesh single-window portal was launched in 2018.
Correct sequence: Mandatory EIA (1994) → Category A/B + SEIAA decentralisation (2006) → NABET accreditation mandatory (2010) → Parivesh Portal (2018), matching option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Options (b) and (c) suggest that decentralisation to SEIAA and the Category A/B classification were introduced at different times — one before or after the other. In reality, both were co-introduced under EIA Notification 2006. The trap exploits candidates who studied these as separate reforms without connecting them to the same 2006 notification.
solution.final_explanation:
Tracking the evolution of specific features within India's EIA system reveals the layered reform trajectory.

**Correct sequence:** 1994 → 2006 → 2010 → 2018

• **1994:** EIA Notification 1994 made environmental impact assessment mandatory for the first time for 29 categories of projects — all appraised centrally.
• **2006:** EIA Notification 2006 simultaneously introduced: (i) Category A (central MoEFCC/EAC) and Category B (state SEIAA/SEAC) classification; and (ii) Decentralisation to state-level appraisal authorities — these two features were co-introduced, not sequential.
• **2010:** MoEFCC made NABET-QCI accreditation mandatory for EIA consultants preparing reports for Category A and B1 projects — a quality-control reform.
• **2018:** Parivesh Portal launched as the single-window digital clearance platform integrating EC, FC, CRZ, and Wildlife clearances.

• Option (a): Incorrect — reverses 2006 and 2010 order.
• Option (b): Incorrect — implies decentralisation preceded Category system, both are 2006.
• Option (c): Incorrect — misplaces NABET as pre-2006.

Value Addition:
• EIA 1994 covered only 29 project types; EIA 2006 expanded coverage significantly.
• The 2006 decentralisation was intended to reduce MoEFCC's workload and speed up appraisal.
• Stage II FC requires EC to be obtained first — sequential clearance rule for forest-located projects.

solution.concept_anchor: SPCB conducts public hearing; 45-day timeline; industrial estate exemption from unit-level hearing
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) attributing public hearing conduct to MoEFCC is deceptive because MoEFCC is the appraisal authority and prominently associated with the EIA process, leading candidates to assume it also conducts hearings.
elimination_logic: Identify the nodal agency question: public hearings are conducted by SPCB/UTPCC, not MoEFCC — eliminate option (a).

Identify the industrial estate provision: in an industrial estate, public hearing occurs at the estate level, not for each individual unit — eliminate option (b) which implies unit-level hearing is required.

Confirm that SPCB must complete the public hearing within 45 days of receiving the SPCB's request, with 30-day prior public notice — option (c) correctly identifies both the SPCB as the conducting authority and the unit-level exemption for industrial estate projects.
Eliminate option (d) — reducing consultation to 10 days is a fabricated timeline not found in EIA 2006.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (a) exploits the understandable confusion between MoEFCC (which appraises the EIA and grants EC) and SPCB (which conducts the public hearing). Both are prominent regulatory bodies in the EIA process, and candidates who have not specifically noted the division of functions will attribute hearing-conduct to MoEFCC. The industrial estate exemption for unit-level hearings is an additional layer of precision that tests nuanced knowledge.
solution.final_explanation:
The Public Consultation stage requires precision about who conducts the hearing and what exemptions apply.

In the scenario: a chemical unit applying for EC within an established industrial estate in a non-ecologically sensitive area falls under a specific procedural provision of EIA 2006.

• Option (a): Incorrect. MoEFCC is the appraisal authority for Category A projects — it receives public hearing records and EIA reports. But the public hearing itself is conducted by SPCB/UTPCC, not MoEFCC.
• Option (b): Incorrect. EIA 2006 provides that for projects within industrial estates, public hearing is conducted at the estate level during the estate's own environmental appraisal — individual units within the estate are exempted from conducting separate unit-level public hearings.
• Option (c): Correct. The State Pollution Control Board (SPCB) is the nodal agency conducting public hearings. It must do so within 45 days of receiving the request. For individual units within an approved industrial estate, the estate-level public hearing satisfies the requirement — no fresh unit-level hearing is needed.
• Option (d): Incorrect. No provision for a 10-day abbreviated hearing exists under EIA 2006.

Value Addition:
• SPCB must give 30-day prior notice in two national + two local newspapers before public hearing.
• Written representations from the public can also be submitted within the 30-day notice period.
• Export Processing Zones and Special Economic Zones follow a similar estate-level hearing model.

Environmental Clearance (EC): Grant, Conditions, and Post-clearance Monitoring

solution.concept_anchor: EAC advisory not decision-making; EC non-transferable; HYCR public disclosure

statement_analysis.statement: The Expert Appraisal Committee (EAC) grants Environmental Clearance directly to Category A projects after completing its appraisal — MoEFCC's role is limited to formal notification of the EAC's decision.
statement_analysis.reason: EAC is strictly an advisory body. It evaluates EIA reports and recommends outcomes, but the formal Environmental Clearance is issued by MoEFCC for Category A projects. MoEFCC's role is substantive, not merely administrative.

statement_analysis.statement: If a project proponent sells the project to another entity after obtaining Environmental Clearance, the EC is automatically transferred to the new owner since it is attached to the site rather than the proponent.
statement_analysis.reason: EC is both site-specific AND party-specific. It cannot be transferred to another entity automatically — transfer requires a fresh application to the competent authority.

statement_analysis.statement: Half-Yearly Compliance Reports submitted by project proponents under EC conditions must be placed in the public domain, enabling civil society scrutiny of post-clearance environmental performance.
statement_analysis.reason: EIA 2006 and MoEFCC directions require HYCR to be submitted to MoEFCC and Regional Offices and publicly disclosed — this is a transparency mechanism in post-clearance monitoring.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) identifying only Statement 2 as not correct tempts candidates who know EC is non-transferable but accept Statement 1's partial truth (EAC does decide outcomes, though they conflate advisory recommendation with formal grant).
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1 — EAC recommends but MoEFCC formally grants EC; describing MoEFCC's role as merely 'formal notification' is incorrect; Statement 1 is NOT correct.
Evaluate Statement 2 — EC is party-specific; automatic transfer is impermissible; fresh application required; Statement 2 is NOT correct.
Evaluate Statement 3 — HYCR public disclosure is a genuine EIA 2006 transparency requirement; Statement 3 IS correct.
Statements 1 and 2 are NOT correct — option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 exploits the association between EAC and EC outcomes. Since EAC evaluates, recommends, and its recommendations are almost always followed, candidates conflate EAC's advisory role with decision-making authority. The precise distinction — that MoEFCC (not EAC) formally grants EC — is the kind of institutional precision that separates well-prepared candidates from those with general knowledge.
solution.final_explanation:
The appraisal stage and post-clearance monitoring involve careful institutional division of roles.

• Statement 1 — NOT correct: EAC is an advisory body composed of sectoral and environmental experts. It evaluates EIA reports, public hearing records, and other inputs, then recommends one of four outcomes (grant EC / EC with conditions / reject / return for more information). However, the Environmental Clearance order is formally issued by MoEFCC for Category A projects. MoEFCC's role is substantive legal decision-making, not mere notification.
• Statement 2 — NOT correct: Environmental Clearance is both site-specific and party-specific. When a project changes hands through sale or transfer, the new entity cannot assume the EC automatically. A fresh application must be submitted to the competent authority. This prevents circumvention of the appraisal process through corporate restructuring.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Post-clearance monitoring requires project proponents to submit Half-Yearly Compliance Reports (HYCR) to MoEFCC and its Regional Offices. These reports must be made publicly available — a mechanism intended to enable civil society and affected communities to track compliance.

Value Addition:
• EAC is chaired by an independent expert, not a serving government secretary.
• Possible EAC outcomes: EC granted / EC with conditions / returned for additional information / rejected.
• NGT has used HYCR data in contempt proceedings against defaulting project proponents.

solution.concept_anchor: ESZ escalation rule; Forest Clearance Stage I/II sequence; T.N. Godavarman 10 km ESZ
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) incorrectly matches T.N. Godavarman case with Forest Conservation Act rather than the ESZ/Protected Area buffer order, exploiting the case name association with forests generally.
elimination_logic: Evaluate A: Ecologically Sensitive Zone (ESZ) projects — projects within ESZ are escalated to Category A regardless of their scale/capacity; A matches 3.
Evaluate B: T.N. Godavarman case — Supreme Court mandated a minimum 10 km ESZ around all National Parks and Wildlife Sanctuaries as an interim measure; B matches 1.
Evaluate C: Stage II Forest Clearance — can only be obtained after Environmental Clearance is granted; Stage I (in-principle) is concurrent; Stage II is sequential post-EC; C matches 4.
Evaluate D: Parivesh Portal — provides common application interface for EC, FC, CRZ, Wildlife clearances; each clearance remains legally independent; D matches 2.
Correct combination: A-3, B-1, C-4, D-2 — option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The T.N. Godavarman case is extensively associated with forests and the Supreme Court's forest governance jurisprudence. Candidates may conflate it with a Forest Conservation Act ruling rather than the specific ESZ buffer zone mandate. The 10 km ESZ interim order in Godavarman is a precise detail that requires knowing the case's specific holdings beyond its general forest governance role.
solution.final_explanation:
This question maps four distinct elements of India's EIA-related clearance architecture.

**Correct matches: A-3, B-1, C-4, D-2**

• A (ESZ-located projects) — 3: Any project located within an Ecologically Sensitive Zone (ESZ) is automatically escalated to Category A for EIA purposes, regardless of its scale or capacity that would otherwise qualify it as Category B.
• B (T.N. Godavarman Supreme Court case) — 1: The Supreme Court in this landmark case directed that a minimum 10 km ESZ be maintained around all National Parks and Wildlife Sanctuaries as an interim protective measure, pending formal ESZ notifications under the EP Act.
• C (Stage II Forest Clearance) — 4: Under the concurrent processing reform, Stage I (in-principle) Forest Clearance can be obtained simultaneously with the EC application. However, Stage II (final approval for actual diversion of forest land) can only be granted after the Environmental Clearance has been issued — ensuring EC conditions inform the forest diversion conditions.
• D (Parivesh Portal) — 2: Parivesh is a single-window digital application platform. It integrates the application process for EC, FC, CRZ, and Wildlife clearances but does NOT merge them — each clearance is independently processed and granted by the respective authority.

Value Addition:
• ESZ notifications are issued under Section 3(2)(v) of EP Act 1986.
• Formal ESZ notifications often specify varying widths (not uniformly 10 km) based on local ecology.
• Parivesh was developed by NIC under MoEFCC and launched in 2018.

National Green Tribunal (NGT) and EIA: Appellate Jurisdiction

solution.concept_anchor: EP Act 1986 penalty caps; NGT independent penalty power

statement_analysis.statement: Under the Environment Protection Act 1986, the maximum fine for violating environmental standards is fixed permanently at ₹1 lakh with no provision for enhancement beyond this ceiling.
statement_analysis.reason: EP Act 1986 provides for a base fine of up to ₹1 lakh, but for continuing violations, an additional ₹5,000 per day is levied for each day the violation continues — the ceiling is not static.

statement_analysis.statement: The National Green Tribunal has the authority to impose penalties and direct closure of projects independently of criminal proceedings initiated under the Environment Protection Act 1986.
statement_analysis.reason: NGT operates as a civil/specialised environmental court with independent authority to impose civil penalties, compensation, and restoration orders — these are concurrent remedies with, not dependent on, criminal prosecution under EP Act 1986.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) claiming both statements are correct tempts candidates who know ₹1 lakh is the base penalty figure and may not know the ₹5,000/day continuation clause that makes the fine extendable beyond ₹1 lakh.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1 — EP Act 1986 penalty: up to ₹1 lakh base fine PLUS ₹5,000/day for continuing violations; the claim of a 'permanent ceiling at ₹1 lakh' ignores the daily extension clause; Statement 1 is incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 2 — NGT can impose penalties and closure orders independently of EP Act criminal proceedings; concurrent remedies are available; Statement 2 is correct.
Statement 1 incorrect, Statement 2 correct — option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1's trap is the word 'permanently fixed' and 'no provision for enhancement.' The ₹1 lakh figure is well-known, but the ₹5,000/day continuing violation clause is the detail that breaks the 'fixed ceiling' claim. Candidates who have memorised only the headline penalty figure without the continuation provision will accept Statement 1 as correct. The scope-extension lies in 'permanently' and 'no provision' — converting a partially true fact into a false absolute claim.
solution.final_explanation:
India's environmental enforcement framework has both a legislative penalty track (EP Act 1986) and a tribunal remedy track (NGT).

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: The Environment Protection Act 1986 provides for imprisonment up to 5 years and/or a fine up to ₹1 lakh for the initial violation. However, for continuing violations — where the offence persists after conviction — an additional fine of ₹5,000 per day applies for each day the violation continues. The ₹1 lakh figure is not a permanent ceiling; the daily extension makes total fines open-ended based on duration of non-compliance.
• Statement 2 — Correct: NGT operates as a specialised environmental court. Its authority to impose penalties, order compensation to affected parties, and direct project closure under the NGT Act 2010 is independent of and concurrent with criminal proceedings under EP Act 1986. A project proponent can simultaneously face NGT civil penalties and criminal prosecution under the EP Act.

Value Addition:
• EP Act 1986 violation: Section 15 provides the penalty provisions.
• NGT's compensation orders are based on the 'polluter pays' and 'public trust' doctrines.
• Chronic under-staffing in MoEFCC Regional Offices limits field enforcement effectiveness — a significant governance gap.

solution.concept_anchor: EIA report executive summary in local language; NABET accredited consultants mandatory
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) attributing accreditation to BIS (Bureau of Indian Standards) is deceptive because BIS is India's most prominent standardisation/accreditation body and candidates unfamiliar with QCI-NABET may substitute the more familiar name.
elimination_logic: Recall that mandatory EIA consultant accreditation is through NABET under QCI — not BIS, not ISO, and not MoEFCC directly.
Recall that the executive summary of the EIA report must be available in the local language for public hearing accessibility — not just in English.
Option (c) correctly pairs NABET-QCI accreditation with local language executive summary requirement.
Eliminate (a) — BIS accredits products and management systems, not EIA consultants.
Eliminate (b) — ISO certification is a quality management standard, not the Indian EIA regulatory accreditation system.
Eliminate (d) — MoEFCC does not directly accredit consultants; it has delegated this to NABET-QCI.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: BIS (Bureau of Indian Standards) is India's most recognisable accreditation and standardisation body — it appears in a wide range of product certification and testing contexts. Candidates who know an accreditation requirement exists for EIA consultants but have not specifically studied QCI-NABET will default to BIS as the 'obvious' accreditation body. This entity-swap is effective precisely because BIS is a real, prominent regulatory body in the correct general domain of quality standardisation.
solution.final_explanation:
Two precise procedural requirements govern EIA report preparation and accessibility.

• Option (a): Incorrect. Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) accredits products, laboratories, and management systems. It has no role in accrediting EIA consultancy organisations. The relevant accreditation body is NABET under QCI.
• Option (b): Incorrect. ISO certification is an international quality management standard applicable to organisations broadly. EIA consultant accreditation in India is governed specifically by the NABET scheme of QCI, not by ISO alone.
• Option (c): Correct. Since 2010, only consultancy organisations accredited by NABET (National Accreditation Board for Education and Training) under the Quality Council of India (QCI) are permitted to prepare EIA reports for Category A and B1 projects. Additionally, the executive summary of the EIA report must be made available in the relevant local language to enable public participation during the hearing.
• Option (d): Incorrect. MoEFCC does not maintain its own consultant accreditation register. It has delegated this function to QCI/NABET.

Value Addition:
• NABET accredits organisations, not individual consultants — the firm must meet quality and expertise criteria.
• QCI is a non-statutory body — a joint initiative of Government of India, CII, FICCI, and ASSOCHAM.
• The structural conflict of interest — proponent paying consultant — remains an unresolved governance gap.
